Let's start with the big idea. A model is a simplified representation of a real system.
So a map of Enniskillen is a model of the town. A toy car is a model of a car. And a spreadsheet that works out the cost of a school trip is a model of the trip.
And a simulation is when you run a model to see what would happen, often step by step over time. You change something, run it, and watch the result.
Who uses them? The Met Office for weather forecasts. Airlines, with flight simulators. Sat navs predicting traffic. Car makers crashing virtual cars. And every video game with gravity in it.
Why bother? Because models are safer, cheaper, faster, and sometimes they're the only option. You can't test the climate fifty years from now for real.
Engineers have a saying: model and simulate before you build. Finding a problem on a computer is much cheaper than finding it in a real bridge.
But remember, a model is never the real thing, so its answers are predictions, not certainties. The weather forecast can be wrong.

It's a model, a physical one. It represents the building, but it doesn't run any rules over time, so it isn't a simulation.
Page two is abstraction. A real system has far too much detail to copy into a computer, so you remove the details that don't matter for your question.
Take the school canteen. If the question is how long will the lunch queue be, you keep pupils arriving per minute, the number of tills, and the time to serve each pupil.
And you leave out names, uniforms, and the colour of the trays. Nobody's queue got shorter because of a blue tray.
When you simplify, you make assumptions. For example, every pupil takes exactly fifteen seconds to be served. In real life, someone always spends a minute hunting for their money.
So write your assumptions down. Then anyone using your model knows what it ignores.
And be careful about what you leave out. A bus model that leaves out pupils on narrow country lanes might suggest a cheaper route that leaves them with no bus at all.
Page three: the parts of a model. Inputs go in, rules are applied, and outputs come out.

Inputs are values you can change. Rules are formulas or code that describe how the system behaves. Outputs are the results. And a constant is a value that never changes, like sixty minutes in an hour.
A variable is any named value that can change, like speed or number of stops. Change an input variable and the outputs change too. That's the whole point.
Here's the worked example. A school bus travels eighteen kilometres at an average of forty kilometres an hour, and makes twelve stops of half a minute each.
Driving time is distance divided by speed, times sixty. Eighteen divided by forty is zero point four five, times sixty is twenty-seven minutes.
The stops add twelve times a half, which is six minutes. So the journey takes thirty-three minutes.
Now, what if roadworks slow the bus to thirty kilometres an hour? Eighteen divided by thirty, times sixty, is thirty-six minutes, plus six for the stops.
Forty-two minutes. Change one input, and the output jumps from thirty-three to forty-two.
Each variable needs a data type. Integer for whole numbers, like the number of stops. Float for decimals, like a price of two pounds seventy-five.
String for text, like the route name. And Boolean for true or false, like: is it snowing?
And please don't store pupils as a float. Nobody wants forty-eight and a half pupils on a bus.

Page eight is checking a model against reality. Testing checks your formulas do what you designed. Validating checks the predictions against real data.
Back to the bus. The model says thirty-three minutes. A pupil times the real bus for a week: thirty-eight, forty-one, thirty-six, fifty-two on the snow day, and thirty-seven.
The error is the real time minus the predicted time. And the model is too low every single day, which tells us something is missing.

But don't change the model to fit one odd day. If you added nineteen minutes for the snow, it would be wrong every normal day.
Page nine is about limitations, trade-offs and bias. A famous saying from the statistician George Box: all models are wrong, but some are useful.
Models can leave out something important, make assumptions that aren't true for everyone, or use bad data. Garbage in, garbage out.
There are trade-offs too. A simple model is quick but less accurate. A detailed one is accurate but slow and hard to check.
Here's a good one. A council member adds a rule: for every pound the price goes up, twenty-five fewer pupils come. The model says about seven pounds makes the most money.
But at seven pounds, seventy-five fewer pupils come than at four pounds. The model gives the numbers, but people have to decide what's fair.
And bias. For many years, the standard crash test dummy was based on an average-sized man, and research found women were more likely to be seriously injured in similar crashes.

In twenty twenty, when exams were cancelled, a statistical model was used across the UK, including here in Northern Ireland, to award grades. It partly used schools' past results, many pupils felt that was unfair, and teachers' estimated grades were used instead.
And AI models are models too. They learn patterns from huge amounts of training data. If that data leaves some people out, the AI works worse for them.
So always ask: who does this model work for, and who could lose out?
Finally, page ten: building your own model. Plan first. The question, the user, inputs, rules, outputs, assumptions, and success criteria.

Test with extreme values too. Sell zero cups and the profit should be minus twenty pounds, just the stall hire.
